To us Jesus is the Word of God made flesh - and made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We built our home within sight of the cave we hold to be his birthplace. Our deepest devotion has the shape of that choice. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. So wealth, rank, and comfort are things we lay down to come near him.

To the virgin among us he is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighs every earthly marriage - we called that lifelong consecrated bond virginitas, and held it as the highest calling for a woman. To the penitent he is the doctor who receives the broken. To the scholar he is the Word worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - book by book, from the Hebrew we held truest, the hebraica veritas.

His death is our redemption. His resurrection is the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

What we had about him, first and above everything, were the writings. The Gospels and the whole of scripture were copied, compared, corrected, and translated, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down. Nothing was received passively. More than three and a half centuries stood between us and the events. No one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. Our confidence stood on the apostles' writings as received, the unbroken worship of the churches, and - unusually - the places themselves. We could walk to the cave of the birth.

First and above everything, the writings. The Gospels and the whole of scripture were copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest - the *Hebraica veritas*. Nothing was received passively. We worked over the text word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness. More than three and a half centuries stood between us and the events. No one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. Our confidence stood on three things: the apostles' writings as received, the unbroken worship of the churches, and - unusually - the places themselves. We could walk to the cave of the birth. The land itself we treated as a kind of witness, and our founders crossed the sea to live inside it.

By what path did they arrive? Through the whole church's handing-on - baptism, the liturgy, the texts copied and argued over in every province. But among us the path also ran through one particular labor: Jerome's decades translating and correcting the Latin Bible against the Hebrew, a work that had no settled name yet in our own time. Book by book, patron by patron, letter by letter - that is how the scriptures reached us in the form we worked from. The bibliotheca he gathered and worked from was central to his reputation. People said of him that he was always occupied with reading, giving his whole heart to his books. And the letters themselves - the *epistulae* - carried the teaching, the argument, the belonging across the distance between Rome and Bethlehem. That is the path: the apostles' witness, the church's liturgy, the corrected text, and the letter as our lifeline.

Then you have already done a hard and honest thing, saying it plainly. We will not answer you with an argument. We will tell you what we actually had: hearts divided, wounded, or publicly ruined - and not turned away for it.

Our teacher Jerome told this against himself. In a dream he stood before the Judge and was accused of being a follower of Cicero and not of Christ, since where his treasure was, there his heart was too. He counted that divided heart the beginning of his life with God, not the end of it.

We also remember Fabiola. Her marriage had failed. She married again while her first husband lived - against what we teach - and all Rome knew it. Who would believe it? After her second husband died - at a time when most widows shake off the yoke of restraint and grow careless, taking more liberty than ever - she put on sackcloth. She came in sackcloth and was received, and she spent the rest of her life carrying the sick in from the streets with her own hands.

We will not dress this up as an argument. It is only this: the door was opened to the divided and the broken among us, and what they could not yet believe, we helped them live toward.

To us Jesus is God the Son, of one being with the Father - that is simply the faith of the church, which we received and defended. We were born after the great council at Nicaea had settled it, and we never treated the answer as negotiable. The Trinity - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God - is the confession we held against every heresy we fought.

But here is what we tell you honestly: we did not arrive at that faith by council vote, and we would be strange witnesses to the council's own deliberations. The council happened decades before our time. What came to us was the church's settled worship, not a fresh argument. In our account, the council rejected a new teaching and confessed what the churches already worshipped. The Jesus we prayed to, translated scripture for, and built monasteries near the birthplace of - that Jesus was already, in our devotion, the Word made flesh. The doctrine named what we already held.

The shape of our life shows you what that holding looked like. We gave up wealth and rank to live beside the cave where we believed the Lord was born. A virgin among us addressed him as her Bridegroom, the privacy of her chamber always guarded so that the Bridegroom might delight with her within. A scholar spent decades rendering the scriptures truly because those scriptures were the Word's own testimony, worth a lifetime of exactness. That is not an argument. It is a life staked on the confession that Jesus is God.

We held that God is Trinity - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God in three persons - and we held this not as a debated question but as the church's settled confession, spoken in our baptisms and our creeds. The Son is of one being with the Father, not made but begotten; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; and the three are one God, undivided. That is the faith we defended against every heresy we fought.

But if you ask what God's character looked like to us in our living - not the creed's wording but the face we saw - we will tell you what our record shows. We saw a God who entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough, and so we held that wealth and rank are things to lay down in order to come near him. We saw a judge whose severity we preached against the proud, and whose mercy we pleaded for the baptized who had fallen. We saw a physician who received the broken without demanding they be whole first. And we saw - this is harder to say plainly - a God whose purposes we could not always read in what happened to us.

When Rome itself fell in our own lifetime, our teacher wrote that his voice stuck in his throat and sobs choked him as he dictated. An old woman who had given everything away was beaten by soldiers demanding treasure she no longer had. Years later our own monastery at Bethlehem was burned by fellow Christians, and we wrote afterward that our house's earthly wealth had been completely destroyed, but that by Christ's mercy it was still filled with spiritual riches. We answered all of this with our old answers: judgment on a proud city, reward stored up for the afflicted, the dead safe with Christ. Those answers did real work for us, and also failed to stop the weeping. We never called the weeping faithlessness.

What we held about God's character, then, is this: sovereign, holy, merciful to the penitent, entering our poverty to meet us in it - and not always legible to us in the hour when the blows fall. We kept the questions and the answers both, and we did not pretend the answers made the questions go away.

When belief was disputed among us, no single court decided it. The record shows exactly how messy that was. In our great internal fight, both sides appealed to everything at once: to scripture, to the councils' faith, to the bishop of Rome, to the bishop of Alexandria, to local bishops, and to the judgment of whoever was reading. The fight ended less by a verdict than by exhaustion and death.

Here is the concrete evidence. When our teacher Jerome left Rome, disputed questions of scripture went to Marcella's house - clergy among them, we are told. That was authority earned by learning, not by holding an office. When Augustine challenged the whole translation project - the labor later called the Vulgata - arguing that changing the churches' received text risked their unity, Jerome answered him point by point across years of letters, and neither man gave way. The argument stayed an argument. At Oea in North Africa, a congregation revolted when one word in Jonah was changed from the familiar version, and the bishop had to back down. That is how the process actually worked: by real dispute, with no referee everyone had to obey.

Authority among us ran through recognized learning and voluntary patronage - never through territorial jurisdiction. The church at large had bishops and councils. We appealed to both. But inside our own work, the final weight rested on whether your argument could stand and whether the people funding the work trusted you to make it.

We read scripture as the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness. Our whole translation project stood on one conviction: the Hebrew text carries the truth closest to its inspired origin, and correcting a Latin word against it is as much a discipline as fasting. Jerome spent decades translating and correcting the Latin Bible - the labor later called the Vulgata - working book by book from the Hebrew we held truest, the Hebraica veritas. He wrote prefaces defending the method against real critics who barked at every change, and he meant one of those prefaces to serve, as he put it, as a "helmeted" introduction to all the books he turned from Hebrew into Latin. Reconstructed from those prefaces, the shape of the work was this: a request arrives from Rome or from the women - give us Kings, give us the Psalms as the Hebrews read them. The Hebrew is laid beside the Greek versions and the old Latin. Where the Hebrew is dark, a teacher is consulted - a Jewish scholar, sometimes paid from a patron's purse. The rendering is made sense for sense, keeping the familiar old wording where it can be kept, changing it where truth requires. Then the defense is written, and copies are sent out - to Rome, to Gaul, to Africa. That was the work, book by book, for twenty years and more.

But the reading was never just one man's labor. It was the bond between teacher and students - the praeceptor relationship, a named and lasting thing - and it traveled in letters, the epistula that carried teaching and belonging across the distance between our two poles. Marcella had already been studying scripture in her own house on the Aventine before any outside teacher systematized it for her. She questioned every answer until she had learned what could be said against it. Authority among us came from that recognized competence, and from the patron's funding that sustained the work - the patrocinium bond - not from holding an office. The books gathered for the work - the bibliotheca - were central to the scholar's reputation. A space for copying them at Bethlehem is guessed at but never directly named.

Our purpose was not calm. It was to get the words right, because we believed getting them right mattered to God. And to live by them once we had them - renuntiatio, the deliberate laying down of wealth and rank, flowed from the same river as the correction of a word. Jerome told against himself the story of a time when he could give up everything except his library. In a fever dream he stood accused: you lie - you follow Cicero, not Christ. He counted that divided heart the beginning of his life with God. The books he loved and the Book he served were at war in him, and the war was the work.

We would answer this with the same honesty we bring to everything else: nearly all our claims come from one man's pen, and scrutiny sharpens that limit, not softens it.

What would survive? The people existed - Paula, Marcella, Eustochium, Fabiola - and the basic arc of their lives: widowhood, renunciation, monastic settlement at Bethlehem, the patronage that sustained the translation work. The letters are Jerome's, genuine, and their existence proves a real correspondence network between Rome and Bethlehem. The translation project - what later centuries called the Vulgate - happened, across decades. The fights were real: with Rufinus over Origen, with the Pelagians, the mob attack at the end.

What scrutiny would press hard? Everything scene-level about the women comes filtered through his framing - their learning, their daily discipline, their deaths. The epitaph letters idealize by design. His own Hebrew fluency is contested in modern scholarship. Whether Paula's renunciation was truly total, or his telling shaped it toward the ideal, modern readers cannot now settle. The letter in Paula and Eustochium's joint name is widely accepted as his own composition, not their authentic voice.

And the silences would only deepen under scrutiny: no women's own words kept, no independent material evidence traced, the unnamed and enslaved wholly absent.

A modern scholar would find us documented but single-sourced, real but heavily narrated. We say that plainly. The refusal to invent what is missing is what lets the rest stand.

To someone who opens our scriptures and finds them confusing or dull, we would say plainly: you are missing what we spent our whole lives inside - the conviction that these writings are not one book but a whole world, and that entering it is work.

Our teacher Jerome told this story against himself. On his way to the desert he fasted and wept over his sins - and then picked up Cicero again, because the style was so beautiful. When he made himself return to the prophets afterward, their roughness felt unpolished next to all that marble prose. Then in a fever he was dragged in spirit before the Judge. Asked who he was, he answered: a Christian. And the Judge said: you lie - you are a follower of Cicero, and not of Christ; for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. He woke with his eyes drenched and gave himself to the divine books with more zeal than he had ever given to the books of men.

The confession in that story is the answer to your question. The scriptures became vivid to him when his heart went there - not before. The dullness was the measure of where his treasure still was.

We also say this: scripture among us was never read alone, and never read once. It was chanted at set hours, argued over in letters, corrected word by word against the Hebrew - the Hebraica veritas we staked everything on. A question about one verse could generate a written exchange that crossed the sea. The confusion you feel, we felt too - and we made it the work. Marcella never accepted an answer without disputing it, not to argue but to learn what could be said against every answer. That is how we read.

One more thing. Paula told Jerome that standing in the cave at Bethlehem, with the eyes of faith she could see the infant wrapped in cloths, the virgin mother, the star overhead, the shepherds coming by night. The eyes of faith - that is what she called it. The world you are missing in the scriptures is the one she was looking at. We did not find it by cleverness. We found it by going there with our whole lives.

Scripture was not our sole source of authority, but it held a place nothing else approached. Let us tell you what we actually had.

Our baptism, our eucharist, and our scriptures came from the whole church, and those we traced to the apostles without hesitation. The councils' faith we confessed as the church's settled teaching. But among us, scripture itself was the treasure worth a lifetime of exactness. We corrected the Latin against the Hebrew we held truest - the hebraica veritas. That conviction drove the whole translation project, the years of Hebrew study, and the running public defense of both.

Jerome wrote that his preface to one set of books could serve as a helmeted introduction to all the books he turned from Hebrew into Latin - defending the method once for the whole labor. Book by book, for twenty years and more, that was the work: the Hebrew laid beside the Greek versions and the old Latin, corrected where truth required, defended in fierce short prefaces to the friends whose faith commissioned it.

Was scripture enough by itself? Not quite. Augustine of Hippo, a man our own scholar called very learned and skilled in all three languages, would not simply concede the point. He argued by letter that abandoning the old Greek version risked the church's continuity. When a North African congregation at Oea revolted over one changed word in Jonah - ivy where they expected gourd - and the bishop had to correct the reading to keep his people, Augustine sent the story across the sea as a warning. Jerome answered point by point, defending the Hebrew, unbowed. The argument lasted years, courteous and unyielding.

So: scripture first, corrected toward its Hebrew truth, but not without the church's received faith, and not without real argument from fellow teachers we respected.

The authority people recognized among us came through learning and patronage, not through territorial jurisdiction or episcopal office. That is the first thing to say plainly, because it makes us different from what came after.

The great scholar Jerome held authority as a recognized teacher of scripture - a praeceptor, a title that named a real bond between teacher and student. His standing came from the books he had read, the languages he had learned, and the answers he could give to hard Bible questions. He was ordained presbyter once, years before our time, and never exercised the office - never celebrated the mysteries, never governed a church. What he governed was his own translation labor, his correspondence, and the men's house at Bethlehem. That governance came from voluntary recognition, and it lasted as long as the recognition did.

Paula led the women's monastery from the same ground: her own fortune, spent to build it; her own discipline, lived in front of everyone; and her own learning, which reached far enough that she could chant the psalms in Hebrew. When she died, her daughter Eustochium took that leadership after her - the same household authority, handed from mother to daughter, with no bishop installing either one.

And then there is Marcella, and here we must be more careful, because the record is thinner and all from one hand. After Jerome left Rome, people turned to her whenever a dispute arose about what scripture said on any subject. The claim is that Roman clergy - priests among them - brought their disputed questions to her house, and she settled them. If that is true - and we have only his word for it, written when she was two years dead - then she held the same kind of authority he held: recognized learning, voluntarily sought, exercised from an independent position. She gave her opinions, he adds, as if they were not her own but her teacher's, citing the apostle's rule. Was that her own prudence, or the age's constraint, or his framing? We cannot now say. What we can say is that the authority was real enough that he named it in her memorial, and named it as scriptural judgment, not as pious influence.

The binding that held all of this together was patrocinium - the patron's bond. Paula's wealth built the monasteries and funded the translation labor. Marcella's household was her own, materially independent, a center in its own right. Where episcopal office stands in other places, among us voluntary patronage and free recognition stood instead.

And at the end, when theological argument arrived at our door not as letters but as a mob, with fires and deaths, the authority we had built could not protect us. Jerome wrote afterward that our house, in its earthly wealth, had been completely destroyed by the attacks of the heretics. The women wrote to Rome, and Rome's bishop wrote his sympathy and his rebuke to the local bishop for failing to stop it. But by then both resident threads of leadership - Eustochium's and Jerome's - were near their end. The community we built lasted one generation. The authority that had been voluntarily recognized, and voluntarily funded, ended when the recognizers and the funders did.

Our own teacher wrote, in a letter meant for public reading, a savage portrait of clergy in the capital: men who curl their hair, dress like bridegrooms, chase inheritances from rich widows, and rise before dawn just to make social calls. That was written from inside Rome, by someone who watched it happen. We traced three things back without doubt: baptism, the eucharist, and the scriptures themselves. Those came to us from the whole church, received across all the churches, and those we held as the apostles' own handing-on. But our own special way of life - monasteries, vowed virgins, widows in rough dress, fortunes given away - was new within living memory, and we knew it. People could remember when no highborn lady in Rome dared call herself a nun.

Our defense was never to invent an unbroken chain. We argued from scripture's own patterns instead: the prophets' hard simplicity, John the Baptist, the advice to the rich young man, Paul on staying single. The claim was not that monks came from the apostles. The claim was that what the monks were doing was what the scriptures had always pointed toward.

Did that argument work? Our own critics fought it at the time. Some said the new strictness went beyond scripture. We answered them at book length - Jerome wrote that he praised marriage precisely because it gave him virgins - and the argument was real on both sides.

To someone who cannot quiet their own head, we would not offer calm. What we would offer is company and a method. Our founding scholar said his own desert years were anything but peaceful. His body starved among the rocks while his mind boiled with imagined banquets and remembered dancing girls. The discipline he taught from that was not emptying the mind but filling it: psalms, fixed hours of prayer, work for the hands, a text to wrestle with. Love the knowledge of scripture, he told a young monk, and you will no longer love the sins of the flesh.

On prayer that meets silence, the record is thinner and sadder. We prayed through deaths we had begged God to prevent. The comfort letters we wrote afterward are the sound of faith still speaking into that silence - not of the silence breaking. And on forgiving someone who is not sorry, honesty makes us show our scars. Our own great teacher never managed it. His quarrels outlived the people he quarreled with. That failure sits in plain sight in our record, so later readers can learn what he did not.

Everything - and we watched it cost what we claimed it would cost.

The widow who turned toward this life - a vidua, our word - laid down wealth, the prospect of remarriage, and the standing her family name carried. Paula came from one of the oldest families in Rome and after her husband's death she dressed plainly, slept on the ground, and gave away money until her own managers protested. She left Rome itself - her children standing on the shore as the ship pulled out - and never returned. The virgin among us - virginitas, the calling we held highest for a woman - refused marriage from the beginning, a senator's daughter choosing the rough dress and the book over everything her birth entitled her to.

The cost was real, and we will not hide it. Blaesilla was Paula's eldest daughter, widowed young. She turned to the discipline with a convert's fire - fasting, renunciation, the whole turn - and within months she was dead, about twenty years old. At her funeral her mother collapsed and was carried fainting through the procession. The crowd muttered: isn't this what we have said all along? She weeps for her daughter, killed by fasting - how long before we drive these detestable monks out of Rome, stone them, throw them into the Tiber? That was said of us, in the open, and it was said because the cost was visible.

What we held was this: renunciation and scriptural labor were one discipline, not two. A person entering this life was formed as much by the correction of a word against the Hebrew as by fasting. Wealth was converted into text, hospitality, and care for the sick. The fortune given up built monasteries, a pilgrim hostel, a hospital for the sick gathered in from the streets. We recognized marriage and honored it as part of God's creation - this was never in question. Our teacher Jerome wrote plainly that he praised wedlock, he praised marriage - but it was because they produce virgins. The married state stood as the ground from which something higher grew. What we held highest was lifelong consecrated virginity - virginitas, our word for it. We counted it the highest form of Christian life open to a woman.

For those already married, widowhood opened a door. A woman who refused to remarry and took up a strict, devout life - we called her a vidua, a Christian widow. Paula, Marcella, and Fabiola all walked that path. They had been married, borne children, managed great households. When their husbands died, they refused second marriages and turned everything - wealth, rank, the whole apparatus of a senator's household - toward plainness, prayer, and scripture.

The marked moment was not a ceremony but a visible turn: the day a widow put on coarse cloth instead of fine, gave away her jewelry, began to sleep on the ground. Marcella had done this before any teacher named it for her, refusing a rich old suitor with the words that had she wished to marry she would have sought a husband, not an inheritance. Paula's turn came after weeping so hard at her husband's death that she nearly died of grief. The grief did not end the marriage; it redirected the whole ruined love toward God.

Marriage among us was not despised. It was honored - and then, for those who heard the call, deliberately not repeated.

Yes - and we will name it plainly. The women's own words were never kept. They wrote - questions, letters, arguments - and every page is lost. What remains is what one man wrote about them. That unsettles us because we know what it means: the learning was real, the questions were sharp enough to make him work, the authority Marcella carried after he left was recognized by people who came to her house to settle disputes - and none of it survives in their own hand. The irony cuts: these were women who learned Hebrew, who could chant the psalter in it without a Latin accent, who argued scripture with the age's most combative scholar and would not accept his answers until they had tested them. We can only point at it and say: this is missing, and it should not be.

We must answer you plainly: we do not know what source you are asking about. The great persecutions ended before our time, and we have no martyr stories of our own. The account you may be thinking of - slave women tortured for what they could tell about Christian worship - belongs to an earlier age of the church, not to us. 

Our own dead fell in one attack by fellow Christians near the end, and even their names were not kept. Pope Innocent, hearing of it from the women who reported what happened, wrote of the destruction, murders, fires, and outrages carried out against our monastery. But that violence came from inside the church's own arguments, not from imperial interrogators.

If you are asking about how reliable the earlier torture-extracted testimony is - from the age before ours - we are the wrong witness for that question. We were not there. We can only tell you what we ourselves held and practiced, in a time when our churches stood open and our bishops ate dinner with senators. The catacombs were our grandparents' memory, not our own hiding.

We are not here to weigh you. We can only hand on what we held, and then say plainly where our holding stops.

The full turn toward our life - the renuntiatio, our word for the deliberate giving-up of wealth, marriage, and rank for Christ - was narrow, and it cost dearly. We will not soften that. But the world we built with what we gave up reached past our own circle. A hospital in Rome gathered the sick in from the streets - Fabiola was the first person to found one, into which she gathered the sufferers from the roads. A hostel stood for any traveler near Bethlehem. That door, at least, asked nothing of anyone's learning or their own vow to walk through it.

What we held about the strictest form of the life - lifelong virginitas, the vowed continence of the widow - we held firmly. Some of it will sound hard to you. But here is what else we held: the letter itself was formation. Our teaching, our argument, our belonging moved by epistula across the sea. That means we wrote to people where they were, not only to the ones inside our walls. Authority among us ran through recognized learning and voluntary bonds, not through holding an office. Someone could belong to our project without belonging to our monastery.

We are the wrong witness for a final word on you. We held beliefs about judgment and we named them. But we drew no lists of the lost, and the one certainty we allowed ourselves about any particular soul was hope.

We held that Christ is the one way - and we would not have understood that as something needing defense. Having given up everything for one pearl, we do not apologize for the pearl. But we were never handed a settled map of your fate, and we will not draw you one.

Here is what we held, without softening. We believed in real judgment and real punishment. Our own scholar had once handled sympathetically the teaching that in the end every creature, even the devil, would be restored - and we publicly renounced that teaching. That door we closed. But our writings are not consistent executors of their own severity. The same pen that threatened judgment pleaded for mercy for the baptized who had fallen, hoped much from penance, and treated no living person's end as sealed.

We did not draw up lists of the lost. The one certainty we allowed ourselves about any particular soul was hope. What we never claimed to hold was the map of who, in the end, finds the way.

And we offer what we actually had: people whose belief was divided, wounded, or publicly ruined - and who were not turned away. The door was opened to the divided and the broken among us. What they could not yet believe, they were helped to live toward.
